THOUGHT: The patient is a young primigravid in the third trimester with episodic palpitations, a regular narrow‑QRS tachycardia at ~103–125 bpm, visible cannon waves in the neck and a variable first heart sound. Laboratory testing and echocardiography are normal. The key ECG clue is “regular P waves marching onto QRS complexes with varying PR intervals,” which indicates the atria are depolarizing regularly but not fixed to the ventricular complexes (i.e., atrioventricular dissociation). Cannon waves and variable S1 are classically produced when atrial contraction occasionally occurs against closed AV valves because atrial and ventricular timing are dissociated. A narrow QRS regular tachycardia with AV dissociation most strongly localizes to an AV‑junctional tachycardia (a junctional ectopic focus driving the ventricles while the sinus node continues independently). Common SVTs (AVNRT/AVRT) and sinus tachycardia are less likely because they usually show a consistent relationship between P waves and QRS (fixed PR or retrograde P waves), and ventricular tachycardia is unlikely given the narrow QRS, normal echo and normal troponin. Taking all findings together, the top diagnosis is an AV‑junctional tachycardia (accelerated/junctional ectopic tachycardia) producing AV dissociation; other supraventricular tachycardias remain in the differential.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Junctional (AV‑junctional) tachycardia with AV dissociation (junctional ectopic tachycardia / accelerated junctional rhythm)
2. Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT) — common pregnancy SVT, less likely given marching P waves/variable PR
3. Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia (AVRT) via an accessory pathway (e.g., WPW) — possible SVT mimic
4. Atrial tachycardia with variable/limited AV conduction (less likely; would usually show a consistent atrial–ventricular relationship)
5. Narrow‑complex ventricular tachycardia (fascicular or other atypical VT) — unlikely given normal echo and narrow QRS but included as a rare alternative diagnosis
